parts:
Hi all, 

I've mainly used JAGS to build hierarchical GLMs but I thought I'd give Stan a go...

I am trying to fit a non-linear logistic survival regression that attempts to partition the hazard rate into two independent (additive) processes: Z dependent (alpha[i] * exp(beta[i] * Z[i])) and Z independent (ho), while also accounting for variable census lengths. 

My goal is to determine how X1 (a standardised group level covariate) and X2 (an standardised observation level covariate) influence alpha and beta - two parameters which describe the negative exponential effect of Z. Here, alpha must always be positive because the hazard rate can never be negative, and beta must be negative because we assume a hazard rate declines with Z.

I've managed to get the model to compile and sample in rstan. But it seems to be slow and is nowhere near convergence (not that I've let it run for 1000's of iterations yet).

For example, sampling 100 iterations took ~50 minutes per chain with Rhats still in the 10's (not that I expect the model to converge in so few iterations).

I’m guessing this might be due to the large sample size (150,000 observations) coupled with estimating fixed and random parameters…  The model might also be struggling to partition the effects of X1 and X2 between both alpha and beta. 

Parallelising the model will help with the length of time taken a bit... but I was wondering whether there is a more computationally efficient parameterisation of this model? I looked into the 'matt tricks' approach but I didn't really understand it or know how it could be implemented in this model.

The model is below and pseudo data (with X1 and X2 already standardised) is attached. Also the sessioninfo()

Any help/advice would be greatly appreciated.

Cheers

James

parts: My first piece of advice for a large data set and a new model in Stan is to subset the data.  If you have some hierarchical structure stratified subsetting is the way to go to make sure there are some observations per group.  It lets you test the model faster and for some data/prior/model combinations the posterior will be better behaved computationally.  I guess for some models the reverse is true where more data makes it better but it helps to know up-front if you're dealing with one of those.  Once you have something working (converges, reasonable autocorrelation) you can pile on the data and figure out efficiency.  Krzysztof

parts:
Hi, Regarding the model, here are some quick suggestions:
- Instead of using truncated normal for the parameters, could you simply do a normal model on log(alpha) and log(-beta)?  To put it another way, put a normal model on A and B, and then write the A - exp(B)*Z?
- Your model is full of logs and exps which will be slowing you down.  I’m not actually quite sure what’s going on with “inv_cloglog” but I see a log(exp) in your expression.  You are also taking the logs of powers; again, best to just put everything on the log scale so you’re not powering up and logging down all over.
- Ideally with a logistic regression you can use bernoulli_logit; this should be much faster for you.

- If your predictors are discrete, you can bin your 150,000 observations and use the binomal likelihood with one data point per bin

A

parts:
Right --- you could use the logit link function instead of inv_cloglog.
We have optimized for that.
>> p[i] <- inv_cloglog(log(census_length[i]) + log(ho) + log(alpha[i] * exp(beta[i] * Z[i])));

>> y ~ bernoulli(p);

would become:

p[i] <- log(census_length[i])
+ log(ho)
+ log(alpha[i])
+ beta[i] * Z[i]);

y ~ bernoulli_logit(p);

I suppose we could write bernoulli_cloglog at some point, but
I don't know that the inferences are that different from logit.
We also don't have a bernoulli_probit. Even if you insist
on cloglog for some reason, you want to unwind that log(u * exp(v))
into log(u) + v.

Powering up and logging down is very arithemtically unstable.

I'd also suggest lowering the initial step size and increasing the
target acceptance rate (adapt_delta). How you do that depends on
the interface.

I would also second Krzysztof's advice --- always start simpler
and build up to the complex model. Simulate data so you know
you're getting reasonable answers and drop groups if you have to.
You don't want to be debugging and optimizing on a model that
takes 50 minutes and hasn't converged. Then when you have everything
working, try the bigger data and read a chapter of BDA to relax :-)

The non-centered parameterization (what we used to call the "Matt trick")
is described in the manual. It's going to be tricky here because
of your parameterization and truncation.
a0[s] ~ normal(a_GM_grp, a_sd_grp) T[0.0,]; //must be positive

So you can't just do this:

a0_raw[s] ~ normal(0,1);

a0[s] <- a_GM_grp * a_sd_grp + a_GM_grp;

It would be possible with some heroic constraint fiddling and
would probably be a win, but I'd try to get this model working first.

We would've named "a_GM_grp" as "mu_a0" and "a_sd_grp"
as "sigma_a0", not that it matters for anything other than making
the models easier for us to read --- your kilometerage may vary.

The other thing you should do to debug is look at the pairs plot for
your parameters --- if there is near perfect correlation between two
variables, you have identifiability problems that will need to be addressed.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Improving computational efficiency of non-linear hierarchical logistic regression
parts:
Hi Bob and Andrew, thanks for your advice. I’ll think about what this will mean to the model and give it a go. 

Also in trying to explain the maths here I think I found a problem in the original model I posted here. ho should have been included in the log around Z. I've edited it above.

The reason I’m using the complimentary-log-log, loge(− loge(1−p)) link is because it is equivalent to a survival analysis in that coefficients are interpreted as hazard ratios. That is, the hazard for one individual relative to another. It also reduces bias due to long and variable census intervals by allowing census_length to be directly included within the model.

What I am trying to do is fit a competing hazards model using interval-censored data where we don't explicitly know the cause of death but we have a theory that Z may be a primary cause of death and that it's hazard rate will depend on covariates (X1 and X2). As such the overall hazard of an individual, λ, is broken up into two independent hazards λho (z independent death) and λz (z dependent death).

λ(t) = λho(t) + λz(t).

Because I’m dealing with binary (alive/dead) data at variable census lengths I used a cloglog link to model survival as follows:

log(−log(1−Pr(yi,t = 1))) = log(∆t) +log(λho +λz).

 

This produces a standard competing risks survival function:

S(t) = 1-( -∆t * exp(λho(t)) * exp(λz(t))).

 

The reason I logged λho +λz is so that each hazard would be treated independently when estimating the overall hazard. This is why I can't simplify the model above to log(a * exp(b)) into log(a) + b. Because it's actually log((a * exp(b)) + ho). Hope this makes some sense…

Also looking forward to your talk on Tuesday Bob!

James

I'd be curious as to how different cloglog and logit are as link
functions---that is to understand your comment about bias.

I do think you can get much more computational efficiency out of the
model by placing at least weakly informative priors on all of the
parameters that currently get improper priors.

Unfortunately, our CDFs are not super efficient nor are they going
to be very computationally stable near boundaries. And the combination of
distribution plus censoring isn't vectorized. Your model could
probably be rewritten to vectorize, because the sampling statement

y[n] ~ normal(mu,sigma) T[0,]

is equivalent to:

y[n] ~ normal(mu,sigma);
increment_log_prob(log_normal_ccdf(0,mu,sigma));

For N of them, you could do this:

y ~ normal(mu,sigma); // vectorizes all N
increment_log_prob(-N * log_normal_ccdf(0, mu, sigma));

At least I think that's equivalent---you should check my work.

If you have time after the talk on Tuesday, I'd like to sit down
and try to understand your model better. In particular, I'd like
to understand one well enough to put an example in the manual.
For example, I don't see where you're modeling any kind of censoring.

I should clarify my earlier statement. In survival analysis (as far as I understand it)... the Logit is more appropriate for event times that are truly discrete, while complementary log-log is more appropriate for events that can happen at any time but are only observed to occur in discrete intervals... The latter is the situation that I have.
There is also several differences between the two:
1: unlike the logit function the clog log is asymmetrical. For example, a change from 0.25 to 0.5 on the logit scale is the same as from 0.5 to 0.75. However, on the complementary log-log scale, the difference between probabilities of 0.25 and 0.5 is larger the difference between 0.5 and 0.75.
2: The other difference is that the coefficients of a complementary log-log model have a relative hazards interpretation, just like coefficients from a standard Cox survival model.

In practice, the choice is may not be consequential. So I may be able to use a logit... though I need to better understand the maths since I've included census_length as a hazard adjustor..

A typical problem with truncated distributions is that
the truncation was done on a guess and the real value
lies near or beyond a boundary. In that case, you'll see
the samples bunching up near a boundary.

For instance, if the real data is normal(0,100), and you model
with normal(mu,sigma), where sigma is constrained to lie in (0,20),
as we see in some user models, then the estimates are going to bunch
up near 20, when they should be allowed to be larger. This is why
we'd prefer a soft constraint. But a hard enough soft constraint
can have the same problem if there's not much data.

On the other hand, if you have a physical constraint implying
truncation, or are using a distribution that's trunctated (e.g.,
positive like a gamma distribution), then you have to define
constrained variables in Stan. And if you have a scale parameter
like sigma above, it absolute must be constrained to be above 0.
Anything else will just lead to rejections and failures to initialize.

- Bob

It adds curvature around the point you expect the answer to be.
It's hard to negotiate big flat areas.

>> I'll set priors on a_GM_grp, b_GM_grp, a1,a2, b1 and b2 the sigmas... but which type of prior do you recommend? Cauchy priors ( & half cauchy for sigmas)?

One way to do this is with an exp transform as in a GLM
model for a Poisson's mean. You can add constraints
so that (alpha < ho).

>> So maybe I can get rid of that truncation...
>> As for b0... current evidence suggests that it should be negative and as such the truncation is a form of informative prior.

This is the kind of thing we'd inform against --- if the
data makes it negative, it'll be negative. A zero upper
bound does a -log(x) transform, which stretches out the
space near zero, and can make the scales hard for the
sampler negotiate (it has to move further and further as
it gets near zero.
>> Lastly, the model I describe above is a log((exp...) + ho) which I don't think can be simplified.

If you've got an exp inside a log, it can be simplified algebraically
and made more arithmetically stable. Check out the log_sum_exp operation.

log(exp(a) + b) should be coded as log_sum_exp(a, log(b)) for stability.
The problem si that exp(a) will underflow/overflow if a is outside of
(-700,700) or so, but the log_sum_exp form will never underflow or overflow.
>> I have to admit I don't fully understand the 'under the hood' workings of HMC or how the code should be written to optimise it's geometry. Or exactly how changing the step size will help/not help.

The key is thinking about the transformed-to-unconstrainedn space
and that you're moving in it with a discrete step size guided by
the gradient of the -log prob on the unconstrained scale. The manual
has a chapter laying out all the transforms.

- Bob

P.S. Our n_eff estimates are pretty conservative if you're
running multiple chains from diffuse starting points.
